title: To Do or Not to Do
author: Ian Frost
summary: Ian Frost, prompted by a coaching conversation with a colleague, argues that the to-do list -- a tool most school leaders rely on for staying organised -- can actually make leaders less present with the people around them. He recounts a colleague's account of feeling exhausted and distracted in meetings while mentally tracking a growing, unmanageable list of tasks, and connects this to Oliver Burkeman's writing on the modern sense of never having life 'nailed down'. Frost identifies three structural problems with to-do lists: tasks accumulate faster than they can be completed, the desire to tick things off distorts prioritisation toward quick wins rather than what matters, and single-line items often lack the context needed to actually act on them. His alternative is a 'done list' -- reflecting each evening on what was actually accomplished, which meetings were constructive, and what was learned -- paired with a lighter, ongoing capture system (like voice notes) rather than a growing static list. The shift, he argues, has made him more present in the room: more likely to look up, listen, and lead discussions rather than clerking notes with his head down.
points: Frost's central diagnostic claim is that heavy to-do-list use can physically pull leaders out of the room -- heads down, half-listening, worried about the next item -- even while they're technically present in a meeting.

His three named failure modes of to-do lists (accumulation faster than completion, prioritisation distorted toward quick wins, and single-word items lacking actionable context) give leaders a specific diagnostic checklist rather than a vague complaint about busyness.

The 'done list' alternative reframes daily reflection around completed, constructive work rather than an ever-growing backlog, which Frost argues reduces anxiety and self-criticism rather than adding to it.

His closing point -- that this shift is 'less about compliance... and much more about connection' -- reframes personal productivity as fundamentally a relational and leadership issue, not just a time-management one.
quotes: We all use to do lists. For food shopping, reminders for our children, holiday packing and of course at work.
I was exhausted and distracted in meetings, worrying about what was coming up next in my diary. I was unproductive, failing to complete my list of tasks, which just grew day-by-day.
1/ Tasks just keep accumulating. The list compounds, and while it feels good to have got them all down, pretty soon you're swamped.
2/ The desire to tick things off means we don't prioritise well.
Basically, I'm trying to stop worrying and fixating over my to do lists, and replacing this habit with a 'done list'.
By doing this, now when I'm with people, I'm more likely to get my head up and out of the laptop, scan the room thinking about others, listen more carefully, and ask better questions.
It's less about compliance (I mustn't miss anything), and much more about connection, (I see more).
